newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Rao set to appear in heavily guarded court.
newsitem.headline: India's Rao set to appear in heavily guarded court.

text.p: Former Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao is due to appear in a heavily guarded court on Monday to face criminal charges in a case that has shaken the ruling coalition government and driven down stock prices.

Police threw a ring of security around the court house where the former Congress party president, surrounded by a permanent security force of commandos carrying machine guns, was scheduled to arrive early on Monday morning, authorities said.
About 300 police, some with sniffer dogs, will be deployed around the Tis Hazari court complex in central Delhi where Rao was set to face Judge Ajit Bharihoke, they said.
On September 21, Bharihoke upheld a summons ordering Rao to appear in court to face charges in the case involving an alleged attempt to cheat an expatriate Indian businessman of $100,000.
Hours after the judge announced his ruling, Rao quit as head of India's oldest party, saying he was innocent but wanted to protect his party.

Then on Thursday, federal police filed charges against Rao in a separate forgery case involving an alleged attempt in 1989 to tarnish the reputation of V.P. Singh, an opposition leader who later became prime minister.
Rao's legal woes forced a change of guard at the top of the Congress party, which suffered its worst ever defeat in general elections ended in May.
The political turmoil sent shock waves through stock markets, which anticipated trouble for Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left government.

Deve Gowda's 13-party minority coalition depends on Congress's backing to survive against the Hindu nationalist opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which is the biggest single party in the lower house of parliament.
Emboldened by Rao's troubles, BJP leaders forecast a falling out between Congress and the United Front coalition.

BJP president L.K. Advani predicted his right-wing party would win elections in populous Uttar Pradesh state which start on Monday and end on October 7, and that there would be snap general elections in 1997.

Bombay brokers said that given the uncertain political climate, stock prices would likely continue sliding this week. But some political analysts have said Rao's departure could strengthen Deve Gowda's hand as many Congress lawmakers would like to join the coalition government.
Last week, Rao's lawyer said he expected his client, denied legal protection against arrest, to be detained at Monday's court appearance. But Rao could immediately request bail.

Newspapers said Rao was expected to wear a bullet-proof vest to court on Monday. No television cameras or photographers were to be allowed into the court room, and only about a dozen print journalists, agencies said.

Worried about the security arrangements which were being handled by local police, the federal government asked for the proceedings to be moved to a nearby sports stadium, a cavernous exhibition hall or a modern convention centre.
The court was due to take up that request on Monday.

Tihar jail, Asia's biggest prison with some 10,000 inmates, was preparing to take in Rao in case he was put under judicial custody pending trial. The two other co-accused are currently in custody in the same jail.
But Rao could be held at home if put under police custody.

On Saturday, Judge Bharihoke sent former communications minister Sukh Ram, who served in Rao's government until last May, to judicial custody in Tihar jail. Police found more than $1 million in cash in two of Sukh Ram's homes in recent raids.
